standard.title: Line and rotational symmetry
standard.description: Recognise line and rotational symmetry of shapes and create symmetrical patterns and pictures, using dynamic geometric software where appropriate
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify, describe and demonstrate quarter, half, three-quarter and full measures of turn (AC9M2M05) and make and classify shapes (AC9M3SP01). They have not yet formally investigated rotational symmetry or created symmetrical patterns.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise and describe line and rotational symmetry in shapes and create symmetrical patterns using appropriate tools.

nodes.label: Line symmetry
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe lines of symmetry in shapes and pictures.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one line of symmetry in a given shape; explain what makes it a line of symmetry.
nodes.typical_width: Identify all lines of symmetry in a range of shapes; create symmetrical shapes and patterns using paper folding, mirrors or software; recognise asymmetric shapes; explain what a line of symmetry means in terms of reflection.
wider: Investigate lines of symmetry in cultural artefacts from diverse traditions (Islamic geometric art, Aboriginal dot paintings, Central Asian textiles), documenting how many lines of symmetry each pattern has
Explore symmetry in the natural environment on Country/Place — investigating flowers, plants and landscapes and discussing how First Nations peoples observe symmetry in nature
success_criteria: Students can identify and draw at least one line of symmetry for a given shape
Students can explain what a line of symmetry means (the two halves match when folded)

nodes.label: Rotational symmetry
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify rotational symmetry in shapes and describe the order of rotation.
nodes.minimum_width: Test one shape for rotational symmetry by tracing and rotating; identify whether the shape has rotational symmetry and name one rotation that maps it onto itself.
nodes.typical_width: Test and record which rotations produce the same image for a range of shapes; identify the order of rotational symmetry; use dynamic geometry software to test rotational symmetry; connect rotational symmetry to the turn measures from earlier years.
wider: Investigate rotational symmetry in tessellations using dynamic geometric software or generative AI tools — exploring how symmetry constraints produce different families of tessellating patterns
Compare line and rotational symmetry across the same set of shapes, building a systematic record of which shapes have each type and both

response_modes.reason: Students frequently confuse line symmetry with rotational symmetry. A structured investigation comparing both attributes for the same shapes — explicitly asking 'does this shape map onto itself under rotation?' vs 'does it map onto itself under reflection?' — makes the distinction clear.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Rotational symmetry connects to many cultural and natural patterns and provides an authentic context for investigating mathematics across traditions. The cultural artefact context is genuinely engaging and gives symmetry meaning beyond the abstract.
success_criteria: Students can test a shape for rotational symmetry by tracing and rotating, and identify one rotation that maps the shape onto itself
Students can distinguish between line symmetry and rotational symmetry for a given shape
